questions.question: Which of the following would best enable 2,2,4-trimethylpentane to be distinguished from octane?
questions.answer: The two compounds are isomers (both $C_8H_{18}$), so they have the same molar mass (B) and give the same amount of $CO_2$ on combustion (C), and neither reacts with bromine water (D). Their fragmentation patterns in the mass spectrum differ because of the branching (A).
options: Determination of molar mass using gravimetric analysis
Measuring volume of carbon dioxide produced when combusted

questions.question: Separate 20.0 mL solutions of a weak monoprotic acid and a strong monoprotic acid of the same concentration are titrated with NaOH solution. Which of the following will be the same for these two titrations?
questions.answer: Equal volumes of equal concentrations contain the same number of moles of acid, which react 1:1 with NaOH, so the equivalence volume is the same (C). The weak acid has a higher initial pH, a higher equivalence-point pH (basic salt) and a lower initial conductivity.
options: Volume of NaOH required to reach the equivalence point
The conductivity of the initial acid solutions

questions.question: Which of the following reagents would liberate carbon dioxide when mixed with a concentrated aqueous solution of sodium carbonate?
questions.answer: Only a carboxylic acid is acidic enough to react with a carbonate: $2CH_3COOH+Na_2CO_3\rightarrow2CH_3COONa+H_2O+CO_2$ (A). Ethanamine is a base, and ethanamide and ethyl ethanoate are neutral.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions will maximise the yield of dinitrogen tetraoxide? $2NO_2(g)\rightleftharpoons N_2O_4(g)\quad\Delta H=-57.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
questions.answer: The forward reaction is exothermic, so low temperature favours the products. The forward reaction reduces the number of moles of gas (2 to 1), so high pressure favours the products (B).

questions.question: 10 mL of 0.01 mol L$^{-1}$ nitric acid ($HNO_3$) is diluted with 90 mL of water. What is the pH of the resulting solution?
questions.answer: The solution is diluted tenfold, to $[H^+]=0.001\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$, so pH $=-\log(10^{-3})=3$ (C).

questions.question: Which of the following hydrocarbons contains an atom with trigonal planar geometry?
questions.answer: An atom with three regions of electron density has trigonal planar geometry: the $sp^2$ carbons of the C=C double bond in propene (B). Propane and 2-methylpropane have only tetrahedral carbons, and propyne has linear carbons.

questions.question: Ethene reacts with hydrogen gas in the presence of a Pd-C catalyst. Which of the following statements about this reaction is correct?
questions.answer: $C_2H_4+H_2\rightarrow C_2H_6$ (ethane): an addition (hydrogenation) reaction with a single product, and the catalyst is not consumed (D).
options: The reaction also produces a byproduct.
The Pd-C is consumed in the reaction.

questions.question: What is the concentration of $OH^-$ ions (in mol L$^{-1}$) in an aqueous solution in which $[H^+]=2.0\times10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$ at 25 °C?
The name 2-propyl-2-chloro-4,5-dibromopentane does not follow IUPAC conventions. What is the systematic name of this compound?
questions.answer: The longest chain runs through the propyl group: $CH_3CH_2CH_2-C(Cl)(CH_3)-CH_2-CHBr-CH_2Br$, which has seven carbons (heptane), with a methyl branch. Numbering from the $CH_2Br$ end gives the lowest locants (1,2,4,4): 1,2-dibromo-4-chloro-4-methylheptane (D).

questions.question: Hydrogen and iodine react at 500 °C according to the equation $H_2(g)+I_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2HI(g)$. The apparatus shown below is set up (vessel X contains 1 mol $H_2$ and 1 mol $I_2$; vessel Y contains 2 mol HI; the two vessels are the same size). The tap between Vessels X and Y is opened and then the system is left at 500 °C until no further change occurs. Which of the following statements is true?
questions.answer: Once the tap is opened the gases mix freely, so at equilibrium the composition is uniform throughout the combined volume. Because the two vessels have equal volume, each species is present in equal amounts in X and Y (B).
options: X will contain more hydrogen than Y.
X and Y will contain the same amount of HI(g).
X will contain less iodine than Y.
Y will contain more HI(g) than X.

questions.question: An organic compound reacted with concentrated HCl and $ZnCl_2$ to produce 2-chloro-2-methylpentane. What was the name of the original compound?
questions.answer: Concentrated HCl with $ZnCl_2$ (the Lucas reagent) substitutes the OH of an alcohol with Cl. The OH must have been on carbon 2 of 2-methylpentane, so the alcohol was 2-methylpentan-2-ol (C).

questions.question: The following equilibrium exists in bromine water: $Br_2(aq)+H_2O(l)\rightleftharpoons Br^-(aq)+2H^+(aq)+OBr^-(aq)$ (red-brown $Br_2$; the products are colourless). Which of the following solutions could be added to the reaction mixture to cause the red-brown colour of bromine water to fade?
questions.answer: The colour fades if the equilibrium shifts right, consuming $Br_2$. $AgNO_3$ precipitates $Br^-$ as $AgBr$, removing a product and shifting the equilibrium right (C). HCl, KBr and NaOBr add products ($H^+$, $Br^-$, $OBr^-$) and would shift it left, deepening the colour.

questions.question: Which of the following salts has the highest molar solubility?
questions.answer: Using the data sheet $K_{sp}$ values: $CaCO_3$ ($3.35\times10^{-9}$): $s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}=5.8\times10^{-5}$ M. $CuCO_3$ ($1.4\times10^{-10}$): $1.2\times10^{-5}$ M. $PbCO_3$ ($7.40\times10^{-14}$): $2.7\times10^{-7}$ M. $Ag_2CO_3$ ($8.46\times10^{-12}$): $K_{sp}=4s^3\Rightarrow s=1.3\times10^{-4}$ M. Silver carbonate is highest (D).

questions.question: A exists in equilibrium with B according to the equation $A(g)\rightleftharpoons B(g)$. If 1.0 mole of A was allowed to reach equilibrium, how many moles of B would be formed if $K_{eq}$ is equal to 0.40?
questions.answer: Let $x$ mol of B form (the volume cancels as the moles of gas do not change): $K=\dfrac{x}{1-x}=0.40\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{0.40}{1.40}=0.29$ mol (A).

questions.question: Propan-2-ol is heated with concentrated sulfuric acid. Compared to propan-2-ol, the product of this reaction:
questions.answer: Dehydration gives propene. Propene is non-polar (less soluble), has a lower molar mass (42 vs 60), has 3 signals in $^{13}C$ NMR (propan-2-ol has 2) and has no hydrogen bonding, so it has a much lower boiling point (D).

questions.question: A section of a polymer is shown below (the repeating unit has a $-CH_2-$ and a $-C(CH_3)(COOCH_3)-$ in the backbone). Which of the following shows the monomer used to produce the polymer shown above?
questions.answer: The backbone repeats as $-CH_2-C(CH_3)(COOCH_3)-$, so the monomer is methyl methacrylate, $CH_2=C(CH_3)COOCH_3$ (A). Option B lacks the methyl group (methyl acrylate), and C and D are saturated, so they cannot undergo addition polymerisation.

questions.question: If you are comparing this polymer (the polymer in Question 16) to polyethylene, which of the following would be true?
questions.answer: Both polymers are addition polymers (made from monomers with a C=C double bond) and form with no small molecule eliminated (D). A is false because polyethylene is also an addition polymer. In B, the ordered packing of HDPE gives stronger intermolecular forces. In C, this polymer is an acrylic (not a polyester, the ester group is on a side chain).
options: This polymer is an addition polymer while polyethylene is a condensation polymer.
High-density polyethylene would have weaker intermolecular forces as the chains can pack into a more orderly solid.
Being a polyester, this polymer is used to make clothing while polyethylene is used for car tyres.
Both polymers could be made without the elimination of a small molecule.

questions.question: Ammonia ($NH_3$) is a weak base in aqueous solution with an ionisation constant $K_b$. Which of the following represents the ionisation constant for the reaction $NH_4^+(aq)+H_2O(l)\rightleftharpoons NH_3(aq)+H_3O^+(aq)$?
questions.answer: The reaction is the ionisation of the conjugate acid $NH_4^+$, so its constant is $K_a$ of $NH_4^+$, and for a conjugate pair $K_aK_b=K_w$. Hence $K_a=\dfrac{K_w}{K_b}$ (C).

questions.question: Which of the following plots correctly represents the conductometric titration of 0.05 mol L$^{-1}$ $H_2SO_4$ with 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ of the weak organic base ethylamine?
questions.answer: Initially the conductance is high because of the highly mobile $H^+$ ions. As the base is added, $H^+$ is replaced by the less mobile $C_2H_5NH_3^+$ and $SO_4^{2-}$ remains, so the conductance falls to a minimum at the equivalence point. After this, extra ethylamine (a weak base, poorly ionised) adds very little conductance, so the line is almost flat (D). A strong base would give a steep rise (A).

questions.question: Solid calcium chloride is added to 200.0 mL of 0.12 mol L$^{-1}$ potassium sulfate solution at 298 K. What is the minimum mass of calcium chloride required to produce a precipitate?
questions.answer: The precipitate is $CaSO_4$ ($K_{sp}=4.93\times10^{-5}$). It first forms when $[Ca^{2+}]=\dfrac{K_{sp}}{[SO_4^{2-}]}=\dfrac{4.93\times10^{-5}}{0.12}=4.1\times10^{-4}$ M. $n(CaCl_2)=4.1\times10^{-4}\times0.2000=8.2\times10^{-5}$ mol, and $m=8.2\times10^{-5}\times110.98=9.1\times10^{-3}$ g (B).

questions.question:
The table provides thermodynamic data about two bromide salts.

| | $\Delta_{sol}H$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$) | $\Delta_{sol}S$ (J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$) |
|---|---|---|
| LiBr | $-48.8$ | 21.5 |
| KBr | 19.9 | 89.0 |

Compare and explain the solubilities of the two bromide salts at 300 K. You should include calculations in your answer.
questions.answer: Use $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S$ (with $\Delta S$ in kJ K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$). LiBr: $\Delta G=-48.8-300(0.0215)=-55.3$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. KBr: $\Delta G=19.9-300(0.0890)=-6.8$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Both values are negative, so dissolving is spontaneous at 300 K and both salts are soluble. LiBr has a much more negative $\Delta G$, so its dissolving is more favourable (a larger equilibrium constant, $\Delta G=-RT\ln K$), so LiBr is much more soluble than KBr. LiBr dissolves because of a favourable (exothermic) enthalpy change, while for KBr the dissolving is endothermic and is driven by the large increase in entropy.

questions.question: Sulfur trioxide decomposition reaches equilibrium at 200 °C according to the equation $2SO_3(g)\rightleftharpoons2SO_2(g)+O_2(g)$. Use Collision Theory to state and explain the effect, if any, of an increase in the overall pressure.
questions.answer: Increasing the pressure (by decreasing the volume) increases the concentration of all gases, so the particles are closer together and collide more frequently. This increases the rate of both the forward and the reverse reactions. The reverse reaction involves 3 moles of gas of products colliding (2 $SO_2$ and 1 $O_2$), compared with 2 moles of $SO_3$, so its rate increases by more than the forward rate. The reverse rate is temporarily greater than the forward rate, so the equilibrium shifts to the left (towards the side with fewer moles of gas) until the rates are again equal, which gives more $SO_3$ at the new equilibrium.

questions.question: Identify the effect, if any, on the value of $K_{eq}$ if the overall pressure of the system is increased.
questions.answer: No effect. $K_{eq}$ depends only on temperature, which has not changed.

questions.question: A 0.40 mol sample of $SO_3(g)$ is placed in a 2.0 L vessel and allowed to reach equilibrium. Given that $K_{eq}=1.30\times10^{-9}$ at this temperature, calculate the equilibrium concentration of $SO_2(g)$.
Complete the reaction below by drawing the structure of the organic product: but-2-ene reacts with HCl(g).
questions.answer: The HCl adds across the double bond (addition reaction) to give 2-chlorobutane, $CH_3CHClCH_2CH_3$ (drawn as a skeletal formula with Cl on carbon 2).

questions.question: Complete the reaction below by drawing the structure of the organic reactants: the reaction with conc. $H_2SO_4$ and heat produces ethyl propanoate ($CH_3CH_2COOCH_2CH_3$) and $H_2O$.
questions.answer: This is esterification (Fischer esterification), a condensation reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol: propanoic acid, $CH_3CH_2COOH$, and ethanol, $CH_3CH_2OH$. $$CH_3CH_2COOH+CH_3CH_2OH\xrightleftharpoons[heat]{conc.\ H_2SO_4}CH_3CH_2COOCH_2CH_3+H_2O$$

questions.question: Lactic acid $CH_3CH(OH)COOH$ is a weak monoprotic acid ($pK_a=3.85$). Write an equation for the reaction of lactic acid with water.
questions.answer: $CH_3CH(OH)COOH(aq)+H_2O(l)\rightleftharpoons CH_3CH(OH)COO^-(aq)+H_3O^+(aq)$

questions.question: Identify a conjugate acid/base pair from this reaction (lactic acid reacting with water).
questions.answer: Acid: $CH_3CH(OH)COOH$ (lactic acid). Conjugate base: $CH_3CH(OH)COO^-$ (lactate). (Also acceptable: acid $H_3O^+$, conjugate base $H_2O$.)

questions.question: State the equilibrium constant expression, $K_a$, for lactic acid.
questions.answer: $$K_a=\frac{[CH_3CH(OH)COO^-][H_3O^+]}{[CH_3CH(OH)COOH]}$$

questions.question: Calculate the pH of a 0.20 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of lactic acid ($pK_a=3.85$).
questions.answer: $K_a=10^{-3.85}=1.41\times10^{-4}$. Let $x=[H_3O^+]=[\text{lactate}]$: $K_a=\dfrac{x^2}{0.20-x}\approx\dfrac{x^2}{0.20}\Rightarrow x=\sqrt{(1.41\times10^{-4})(0.20)}=5.3\times10^{-3}$ M. $$pH=-\log(5.3\times10^{-3})=2.27\ (\approx2.28\ \text{if the quadratic is solved}).$$

questions.question: You have 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ solutions of each of $NaNO_3$ and $Na_2CO_3$. Predict whether these two solutions are acidic, neutral or basic, explaining your reasoning with chemical equation(s), where relevant.
questions.answer: **$NaNO_3$ is neutral.** It is the salt of a strong acid ($HNO_3$) and a strong base (NaOH), so neither $Na^+$ nor $NO_3^-$ reacts with water. **$Na_2CO_3$ is basic.** $Na^+$ does not react, but $CO_3^{2-}$ is the conjugate base of the weak acid $HCO_3^-$ and acts as a base: $$CO_3^{2-}(aq)+H_2O(l)\rightleftharpoons HCO_3^-(aq)+OH^-(aq)$$ producing excess $OH^-$.

questions.question: Compound X has the molecular formula $C_4H_{10}O$ and is highly soluble in water. It does not react when heated with acidified $KMnO_4$ nor acidified $K_2Cr_2O_7$. Draw the structure and name compound X.
questions.answer: X is a **tertiary alcohol**, 2-methylpropan-2-ol, $(CH_3)_3C-OH$. It is soluble in water (small, with an OH group for hydrogen bonding) and tertiary alcohols are not oxidised by acidified $KMnO_4$ or $K_2Cr_2O_7$ (an ether would also not be oxidised but would not be highly soluble).

questions.question: Predict the number of signals that compound X (2-methylpropan-2-ol) will show in $^{13}C$ NMR.
questions.answer: **2 signals**: one for the three equivalent $CH_3$ carbons, and one for the carbon bonded to the OH.

questions.question: Draw two isomers of compound X that contain the same functional group as compound X (the alcohol OH).
questions.answer: Any two of: butan-1-ol ($CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2OH$), butan-2-ol ($CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CH_3$), 2-methylpropan-1-ol ($(CH_3)_2CHCH_2OH$).

questions.question: Equal volumes of hydrogen and bromine are introduced at $T=0$ minutes to a sealed vessel and allowed to reach equilibrium at 60 °C: $H_2(g)+Br_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2HBr(g)$, $\Delta H=-103\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. The graph shows the concentrations of HBr and $H_2$ against time. Calculate $K_{eq}$ for this reaction at 60 °C.
questions.answer: From the graph, $H_2$ falls from 6 to 2 ($\times10^{-3}$ M) and $HBr$ rises to 8 ($\times10^{-3}$ M). Equal volumes of $H_2$ and $Br_2$ were added so the initial $[Br_2]=6\times10^{-3}$ M, and the same amount reacts: $[Br_2]=2\times10^{-3}$ M at equilibrium (check: 4 mol L$^{-1}$ consumed produces 8 of HBr). $$K_{eq}=\frac{[HBr]^2}{[H_2][Br_2]}=\frac{(8\times10^{-3})^2}{(2\times10^{-3})(2\times10^{-3})}=16.$$

questions.question: At 12 minutes, the temperature was changed. Deduce whether the temperature was increased or decreased and explain the change in concentration of $H_2(g)$ and $HBr(g)$ in terms of activation energy of the opposing reactions.
questions.answer: **The temperature was increased.** After 12 minutes $[HBr]$ fell (8 to 6) and $[H_2]$ rose (2 to 3), so the equilibrium shifted to the left (the endothermic reverse reaction is favoured). For an exothermic forward reaction a rise in temperature favours the reverse reaction, which is consistent with the data (K decreases). **Explanation:** raising the temperature increases the average kinetic energy, so a greater proportion of collisions have energy at least equal to the activation energy, and the rates of both reactions increase. The reverse reaction (endothermic, $\Delta H=+103$ kJ mol$^{-1}$) has the higher activation energy ($E_{a,rev}=E_{a,fwd}+103$), so its rate increases by a greater factor. The reverse rate exceeds the forward rate, so HBr decomposes to $H_2$ and $Br_2$ until a new equilibrium is established with the rates equal again (higher $[H_2]$, lower $[HBr]$).

questions.question: Butan-2-one can be produced from 2-bromobutane in two steps. Complete the reaction scheme to show how 2-bromobutane can be converted to butan-2-one. Include the reaction conditions for each step and diagrams for the intermediate compound and butan-2-one.
questions.answer: **Step 1 (substitution):** 2-bromobutane is heated under reflux with aqueous NaOH (or KOH) to give the intermediate compound, **butan-2-ol**, $CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CH_3$. **Step 2 (oxidation):** butan-2-ol (a secondary alcohol) is heated with acidified potassium dichromate, $K_2Cr_2O_7/H^+$ (or acidified $KMnO_4$), to give **butan-2-one**, $CH_3COCH_2CH_3$.

questions.question: 0.561 g of ethanol undergoes complete combustion. Write a balanced chemical equation for the complete combustion of ethanol.
questions.answer: $C_2H_5OH(l)+3O_2(g)\rightarrow2CO_2(g)+3H_2O(l)$

questions.question: 0.561 g of ethanol undergoes complete combustion using the equipment shown (a can containing 100.0 mL of water, initial temperature 20.0 °C, heated by an ethanol burner). The enthalpy of combustion of ethanol is $-1367\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Assuming half of the energy released from the burner is transferred into the water, calculate the final temperature of the water.
questions.answer: $n(C_2H_5OH)=\dfrac{0.561}{46.07}=0.01218$ mol. Energy released $=0.01218\times1367=16.65$ kJ. Energy to the water $=\tfrac12(16.65)=8.32$ kJ $=8.32\times10^3$ J. Using $q=mc\Delta T$ with $m=100.0$ g: $\Delta T=\dfrac{8.32\times10^3}{(100.0)(4.18)}=19.9$ °C. Final temperature $=20.0+19.9=39.9$ °C.

questions.question: Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA, $C_{18}H_{30}O_2$) is an omega-3, essential fatty acid. Its structure is shown in the diagram below (a carboxylic acid with an 18-carbon chain containing three C=C double bonds at carbons 9, 12 and 15). On the diagram, circle the functional groups of this molecule.
questions.answer: The functional groups are the **carboxyl group** (–COOH, at the left end of the chain) and the **three carbon–carbon double bonds** (alkene groups, C=C, between carbons 9–10, 12–13 and 15–16).

questions.question: Predict whether this molecule (ALA) would be water-soluble, explaining your reasoning.
questions.answer: It would be insoluble (or very sparingly soluble) in water. Only the small –COOH group is polar and can hydrogen bond with water, whereas the long 18-carbon hydrocarbon chain is non-polar and only forms weak dispersion forces. The energy needed to break the hydrogen bonds between water molecules is not recovered by the weak attractions between water and the non-polar chain, so the non-polar chain dominates and the molecule does not dissolve.

questions.question: 2 mL of ALA is mixed with 2 mL of bromine water, shaken and then left to stand for a few minutes. Identify and explain two observations you would make.
questions.answer: **Observation 1:** the red-brown/orange colour of the bromine water fades (decolourises). Explanation: bromine adds across the C=C double bonds of ALA in an addition reaction (ALA is unsaturated), forming a colourless bromoalkane. **Observation 2:** two separate layers form (immiscible liquids), with the organic layer above the aqueous layer. Explanation: ALA is non-polar and insoluble in water and, with a density of 0.91 g mL$^{-1}$ (less than water), it floats on top.

questions.question: When used, ALA is often partially hydrogenated, so it is an unhealthy trans-fat that has a single carbon-carbon double bond remaining. Calculate the volume of hydrogen gas at 100 kPa and 25 °C required to convert 1.0 g of ALA to its equivalent trans-fat. (Molar mass of ALA = 278.4 g mol$^{-1}$.)
questions.answer: ALA has three C=C double bonds; leaving one remaining requires 2 mol $H_2$ per mole of ALA. $n(ALA)=\dfrac{1.0}{278.4}=3.59\times10^{-3}$ mol, so $n(H_2)=2\times3.59\times10^{-3}=7.18\times10^{-3}$ mol. At 100 kPa and 25 °C, 1 mol occupies 24.79 L: $$V=7.18\times10^{-3}\times24.79=0.18\ \text{L}\ (178\ \text{mL}).$$

questions.question: This question is about buffers. State what is meant by the term buffer and describe the chemical composition of an acid buffer solution in general terms.
questions.answer: A buffer is a solution that resists a change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added (or when it is diluted). An acid buffer consists of a weak acid together with its conjugate base (usually as a salt of the weak acid), both present in significant, comparable amounts.

questions.question: 50.0 mL of 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ ammonia solution is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.060 mol L$^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid and the resulting mixture forms a buffer. The $K_b$ of $NH_3$ is $1.78\times10^{-5}$. Describe what would happen if an additional small amount of acid solution was added to this buffer. Use an equation to support your explanation.
questions.answer: The mixture contains $NH_3$ (a weak base) and its conjugate acid $NH_4^+$. Added $H^+$ is consumed by the $NH_3$ present: $$NH_3(aq)+H_3O^+(aq)\rightarrow NH_4^+(aq)+H_2O(l)$$ so almost all the added acid is removed, and since the ratio $[NH_3]/[NH_4^+]$ changes only slightly the pH changes very little.

questions.question: 50.0 mL of 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ ammonia solution is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.060 mol L$^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid. The $K_b$ of $NH_3$ is $1.78\times10^{-5}$. Calculate the pH of the buffer produced when the two solutions were mixed.
Determine the maximum mass of calcium hydroxide that will dissolve in 230 mL of 0.040 M barium hydroxide solution at 25 °C.
Deduce whether a precipitate will form when 5.0 mL of 0.010 mol L$^{-1}$ magnesium sulfate solution is added to 10.0 mL of 0.020 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium carbonate solution at 25 °C.
questions.answer: The possible precipitate is $MgCO_3$ ($K_{sp}=6.82\times10^{-6}$). After mixing (total 15.0 mL): $[Mg^{2+}]=\dfrac{0.010\times5.0}{15.0}=3.33\times10^{-3}$ M and $[CO_3^{2-}]=\dfrac{0.020\times10.0}{15.0}=1.33\times10^{-2}$ M. $Q=[Mg^{2+}][CO_3^{2-}]=(3.33\times10^{-3})(1.33\times10^{-2})=4.4\times10^{-5}$. Since $Q>K_{sp}$ ($4.4\times10^{-5}>6.82\times10^{-6}$), a precipitate of $MgCO_3$ will form.

questions.question: Two organic compounds, A and B, are isomers with a chemical composition by mass of carbon 54.5%; hydrogen 9.2%; and oxygen 36.3%. A is soluble in water, while B is a pleasant-smelling liquid. The mass spectra of both A and B have the $M^+$ peak at 88 but are otherwise not helpful in distinguishing between the isomers as they both show peaks at an m/z ratio of 15, 29, 43 and 73. A's carbon-13 NMR has three peaks (184, 35 and 19 ppm), while B's has four peaks (171, 60, 21 and 17 ppm). The IR and proton NMR spectra are shown below (A: broad IR band centred about 3000 cm$^{-1}$ and a C=O near 1700 cm$^{-1}$; $^1$H NMR: singlet at about 12 ppm (integral 1), multiplet at about 2.6 ppm (1) and a doublet at about 1.2 ppm (6). B: no broad O–H band, a C=O near 1740 cm$^{-1}$; $^1$H NMR: quartet at about 4.1 ppm (1), singlet at about 2.0 ppm (1.5) and triplet at about 1.2 ppm (1.5)), along with proton NMR shift data. Determine the structure of each of the isomers. Draw and name the isomers. Justify your choices based on the information provided, making sure to reference ALL spectral types.
questions.answer: **Empirical formula:** moles per 100 g: C $54.5/12.01=4.54$; H $9.2/1.008=9.1$; O $36.3/16.00=2.27$. The ratio is $C:H:O=2:4:1$, so the empirical formula is $C_2H_4O$ (44). The $M^+$ peak at 88 shows the molecular formula is $C_4H_8O_2$. **Compound A: 2-methylpropanoic acid**, $(CH_3)_2CHCOOH$. IR: very broad O–H stretch (about 2500–3300 cm$^{-1}$) and C=O (about 1700 cm$^{-1}$) show a carboxylic acid (soluble in water). $^{13}C$ NMR: 3 signals — 184 ppm (COOH), 35 ppm (CH) and 19 ppm (two equivalent $CH_3$). $^1H$ NMR: singlet at about 12 ppm, 1H (COOH); multiplet at about 2.6 ppm, 1H (CH split by six neighbours); doublet at about 1.2 ppm, 6H (two equivalent $CH_3$ split by the one CH). Mass spectrum: $M^+=88$; fragments at 73 ($M-CH_3$), 43 ($(CH_3)_2CH^+$), 29 and 15. **Compound B: ethyl ethanoate**, $CH_3COOCH_2CH_3$. IR: C=O at about 1740 cm$^{-1}$ (ester) and no broad O–H band. $^{13}C$ NMR: 4 signals — 171 ppm (C=O), 60 ppm ($OCH_2$), 21 ppm ($CH_3CO$) and 17 ppm ($CH_3$ of ethyl, given as 17 in the question; about 14 ppm is typical). $^1H$ NMR: quartet at about 4.1 ppm, 2H ($OCH_2$, split by $CH_3$); singlet at about 2.0 ppm, 3H ($CH_3CO$, no neighbours); triplet at about 1.2 ppm, 3H ($CH_3$ split by $CH_2$) (the integrals 1:1.5:1.5 correspond to 2:3:3). Ester (pleasant smell, no hydrogen bonding, insoluble) matches the description of B. Mass spectrum: $M^+=88$; fragments 73, 43 ($CH_3CO^+$), 29 ($C_2H_5^+$) and 15.

questions.question: The following graph shows how the pH changes during the titration of 25.00 mL of a solution of a weak monoprotic acid (HA) with NaOH. Using the graph, identify the pH at the equivalence point.
questions.answer: The equivalence point is at the middle of the steep vertical section, at a volume of about 8.1 mL of NaOH. The pH there is about **8.7** (basic, because the salt $A^-$ hydrolyses; accept 8.5–9).

questions.question: Bromocresol purple is an indicator that changes from yellow to violet over the range 5.2–6.6. If bromocresol purple was used to detect the end point of this titration, what effect, if any, would this have on the calculated concentration of HA compared to its actual concentration?
questions.answer: The indicator changes colour at pH 5.2–6.6, which is on the lower part of the steep rise, before the equivalence point (pH about 8.7). The end point would be reached too early, so the measured titre would be too small and the calculated concentration of HA would be lower than its actual concentration.

questions.question: The graph shows the titration of 25.00 mL of a solution of a weak monoprotic acid (HA) with 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH. Calculate the $pK_a$ value of the HA acid. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
questions.answer: From the graph, the equivalence point is at about 8.1 mL: $n(NaOH)=0.10\times0.0081=8.1\times10^{-4}$ mol $=n(HA)$, so $[HA]=\dfrac{8.1\times10^{-4}}{0.02500}=0.0324$ M. The initial pH is 3.0 (graph at 0 mL), so $[H^+]=1.0\times10^{-3}$ M $=[A^-]$. $$K_a=\frac{[H^+][A^-]}{[HA]}=\frac{(1.0\times10^{-3})^2}{0.0324-0.0010}=3.2\times10^{-5}\ \Rightarrow\ pK_a=4.50.$$ Check: at the half-equivalence point (4.05 mL) $pH=pK_a$, and the graph gives pH $\approx4.4$–$4.5$ there. (Values are read from the graph, so the answer is approximate, $pK_a\approx4.5$.)
